text:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, hike the Waptus River Trail about nine miles to Waptus Lake. The hiker bridge over Spinola Creek near the lake has washed out, so cross at the nearby horse ford, reached from the Waptus Pass Trail. Where the trail joins the PCT, head southbound (west).

Shortly before the PCT crosses the Waptus River, leave the trail and head northwest toward a faint shoulder and bench through flat, easy forest. Pick up a fisherman's trail on the southwest side of that bench and follow it toward Shovel Creek, then up and over the bench past an informal campsite with a giant cairn, where it starts to climb the shoulder on the east side of Shovel Creek.

Before long the trail leaves the forest straight onto talus. Easy talus walking brings you to Shovel Creek; cross where convenient.

Roughly 13 miles to the base, five to six hours. Most parties camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge.
runs: joins the pct head southbound west shortly before the pct crosses the waptus river
shovel creek then up and over the bench
talus easy talus walking brings you to shovel creek cross

text:
Crossing Shovel Creek off the talus puts you at the foot of the Mega Slab — that is the arrival, and it is a creek crossing rather than a judgement. The slab drops from the peak's southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft all the way to Shovel Creek at about 3,700 ft, so there is no ambiguity about which piece of rock it is: it is the enormous unbroken sheet above you, one of the longest continuous sandstone slabs in North America.

Which line on the slab is the real question here, and for this route the answer is a single word: lowest. Infinite Beauty begins at the lowest part of the slab, on a shallow rib. Walk the base downhill until it stops going down, and start on the rib there.

How that distinguishes it from its neighbour: Timeless Treasure climbs the middle of the slab. So if you have walked out along the base looking for a nicer-looking start, you are on Timeless Treasure. The lowest point is the whole distinction and it is decidable by walking downhill rather than by looking.

What the rock should feel like, as confirmation: clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone with minimal breaks, and roughly 2,000 ft of sustained fourth class. Approach shoes or trail runners friction well on it and most of the slab is climbed unroped. If you are pulling into cracks or dodging vegetation, you are off the clean sheet.

And where the route ends its own identity: after about 2,000 ft the line naturally angles right and joins Timeless Treasure for brief, unexposed low-fifth moves up overlaps trending up and right to the southeast shoulder. Easy scrambling then leads to the summit block, where the rock quality noticeably deteriorates over the final three pitches.
runs: one of the longest continuous sandstone slabs in north america
at the lowest part of the slab on a shallow rib
moves up overlaps trending up and right to the

text: Ten stoppers, two small cams, and six runners were adequate for the whole route on one recorded ascent. A single 50m rope is enough for the rappels, but 60m or two 50m ropes let 3-person parties reach belay stances more comfortably.
runs: ten stoppers two small cams and six runners

text: Ten stoppers, two small cams, and six runners were adequate for the whole route

text: Sustained 4th-class climbing on clean, low-angle sandstone up the center of the slab, left of the giant corner.

text: From US-2 at the western edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive 8.4 miles, then turn left onto Eightmile Road (FS Road 7601) and follow the rough dirt road 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park and overnight trips May 15 to Oct 31 need an Enchantment permit; the road is usually gated November into May.
runs: dirt road 3.7 miles to the stuart lake trailhead

text: From the summit, descend the north face on four single-rope rappels using a single 60m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground to the climbers’ path; two optional rappels from stations climber’s right of the gully can replace that downclimb. The first rap station is an old bolt at the true summit (reported to predate the 1980s); the second rappel is built around a wedged block that looks sketchy but has held for decades of parties. Remaining stations are slung natural anchors (webbing/tat) — carry extra material to back up aged slings. From the climbers’ path, scramble around to the base of the West Ridge; some parties report one more short rappel from that notch to regain the south-face base. Total time from summit back to packs is roughly 2 hours in a typical trip report.
runs: around to the base of the west ridge

text: Traverse right across the obvious Snafflehound Ledge to a small tree, then a short steep step to the base of the crux pitch.
runs: a short steep step to the base of the crux

text: Crack system/steep gully bypassing a chockstone on the left to the small notch east of the summit horn; watch for loose blocks in the gully.
runs: gully bypassing a chockstone on the left to the small notch east of the summit horn

text: No campfires above 5,000 ft or within 1/2 mile of lakes; dogs prohibited on Colchuck Lake, Stuart Lake trails, and Enchantments area
runs: no campfires above 5 000 ft or within 1/2 mile of lakes

text:
Look for two large Vs and start in the chimney to their left. That is the whole identification, it is published in exactly those terms, and the accompanying note is that you cannot miss it. Two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; the route's first pitch takes the chimney immediately left of them.

Confirm with the first pitch itself: from the chimney you move left and climb up on knobs to a belay, at about 5.7. Knobs after a leftward move out of a chimney is the signature. If you are pulling straight up out of the chimney with no traverse, look again.

Position relative to its neighbour, which is the check that catches the common error: this route is to the climber's right of the classic south-face line. So if you are at the middle of the base of the face, you are one route too far left. Walk right until the two Vs are on your right-hand side and you are at a chimney.

And a distance check on the route as a whole: seven pitches, about 650 ft, running 5.5 to 5.9, with a long chimney-gully crossing to a big ledge partway up and a forced rightward dihedral as the crux. A four- or five-pitch route ending on the West Ridge is one of the shorter lines on the left flank, not this.

In cloud, when you cannot see the Vs from a distance, walk the foot of the face and count chimneys rather than guessing: the Vs are large features and they are visible from close under them even when the summit is not.
runs: move left and climb up on knobs to a belay

text: The route follows a ledge system extending from the center of the south face rightward into a series of chimneys and wide cracks. Lower pitches (roughly pitches 2-4) involve scrambling and chimney climbing from 5.6-5.7 up to 5.8+ on somewhat loose rock. The crux, pitch 5, is a pleasant finger-and-hands crack with good protection, finishing with a fist jam through a small overhang. Some parties continue up the final West Face 5.6 slab pitch to reach the true summit rather than stopping at the top of pitch 6.

rightward into a series of chimneys and wide cracks
is a pleasant finger and hands crack with

text: Stay on the climbers' trail on the west side of the creek and keep heading up-valley through talus and boulder fields to the head of the basin. Turn left (east) and climb broad scree to the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon, aiming for the col midway between them rather than the steeper notch nearer Half Moon, and cross into the basin under Big Kangaroo's south wall. Start up the obvious central ramp and climb six pitches of ramps, chimneys and cracks, 5.4 to 5.9+. From the last belay scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which stands a few hundred feet higher. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches, finishing with the exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old 1/4-inch bolt.
runs: between the south face and the true summit

text: Do not plan to rappel the Beckey-Tate line itself — while it's technically possible with two ropes (roughly five or six rappels off slings and trees), the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, making rope-stuck and rockfall risk high; most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead, from the top of the route scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which stands a few hundred feet higher. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches to the unprotected 5.6 summit slab (protected by a single old bolt), which is downclimbed or top-roped; then descend the shared gully: two slung-block anchors get you down with one or two single-rope rappels (a 60m rope is sufficient either way) through the steep/loose upper gully, after which it's a scree-and-snow walk/glissade down the gully back to the approach basin, across Early Winters Creek, and out the climbers' trail to the Hairpin Turn. Expect the full descent to take a couple of hours; keep helmets on throughout given the loose rock in the gully.
runs: between the south face and the true summit

text:
Cut left, east, toward the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon. That col drops and traverses you into the south-facing basin directly below Big Kangaroo's south wall.

Arrival at the route itself is visual and unambiguous when you can see the wall: the Beckey-Tate's obvious central ramp-and-ledge system splits the face. A single ramp system running up the middle of a south wall, splitting it, is the line.

So the order of finds is: stay west of the creek, reach the head of the basin, cut east to the Half Moon col, drop into the south basin, then look for the ramp splitting the middle of the wall.

The negative test against the west face, which is the commonest error from this car: the west face route crosses Early Winters Creek after only half a mile, at the edge of the talus field, and takes a broad shallow west-facing gully with a chockstone in it. If you crossed the creek early and are looking at a chockstone, you are on the west side of the mountain.

And against the other south-face lines, which share this basin: Kearney-Thomas crosses the creek and ascends the prominent gully system taking the left fork at the high Y-junction. Going down under starts at the Beckey-Tate base and then traverses right across overlaps to its own start ledge. Skinny Start is about 30 metres right of the Kearney-Thomas start. So on this wall: the central ramp is Beckey-Tate, and everything else is measured from either it or Kearney-Thomas.

Descent is not down this route, and the reason matters: rappelling the Beckey-Tate is technically possible with two ropes, roughly five to six rappels off slings and trees, but the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, so rope-stuck and rockfall risk is high and most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which is a few hundred feet higher, and descend the gully from there.
runs: between the south face and the true summit

text: Beyond Redlining climbs the West Face of Vega North Tower (Eros Tower) in 11 sustained pitches (1,200 ft, Grade IV 5.10+; 8 of 11 pitches are 5.10 or harder), topping out on the same summit as Mile High Club. Established by Rad Roberts and Kurt Hicks in July 2020, it is a full grade harder, longer, and more committing than Mile High Club — generally excellent rock, with one notably polished, more run-out pitch (P3) and a long 55m opening pitch.
runs: on the same summit as mile high club

text: Drive to the Sunrise Mine trailhead (Mountain Loop Highway, Forest Road 4065) and start up the Sunrise Mine Trail. Follow it about 2.5 miles, gaining to roughly 4,300 ft, to the last major switchback before the trail begins its final zigzag up toward Headlee Pass — this is the turnoff point, not the pass itself. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up a cairned traverse heading northeast across open talus toward Vega North Tower (also called Eros Tower). The line of cairns crosses two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees, passing just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees. This talus traverse is the shared approach for Mile High Club, Marvin's Ear, and Beyond Redlining, so cairns and a boot path are well established in season, but talus can be loose and slow going with a pack. A reliable fresh-water seep is at a red-rock outcrop in the Mile High gully, roughly at the base of the formation — worth topping off here since there's no water higher on the wall. Beyond Redlining's start is on the dark gray face directly above the two largest boulders at the base of the tower, just left of (west of) Mile High Club's start. Expect lingering steep snow against the base in early season, which can make the last stretch of the talus approach and the transition onto rock its own small crux.
runs: just above a large flat topped boulder near the first

text: A fun slab with easy runout, then steep athletic moves and a punchy crux at a bulge.
runs: steep athletic moves and a punchy crux at a bulge

text: Mountain Project route page confirms: '60 meter rope,' '17 quickdraws,' and '3-6 alpine draws to reduce rope drag'; a 70m rope is a helpful-but-not-mandatory retreat option.
runs: 3 6 alpine draws to reduce rope drag

text: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings are set back from the top of the route, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down to the lower anchor at the base of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.

text: Sunrise Mine trailhead, then the trail for about two and a half miles through the two unbridged creek crossings and up through forest to the last major switchback before the final zigzags toward the pass — leave the trail there, not at the pass. A cairned traverse then runs northeast across talus toward the tower, crossing two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees and passing just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees. The boot path is well established in season because three routes share it. Top up water at the seep by the red-rock outcrop in the gully; there is none higher.
runs: just above a large flat topped boulder near the first

text: Leave the Wildhorse Creek Trail at about 5,400 ft, directly west of the summit. Climb east through meadows, going around the rock bands rather than through them, to gain the west ridge. Follow the ridge east toward the main summit ridge. Short of the summit headwall, turn north and traverse below it, then scramble up blocky Class 2-3 ledges to the summit pinnacle. The last moves are exposed; pick the easiest line and test holds, as the rock is broken and loose in places.
runs: 5 400 ft directly west of the summit

text: From Highway 20 in Winthrop, turn north on West Chewuch Road, go straight at the junction with East Chewuch Road after about 7 miles, continue about 2.5 miles as the road becomes Forest Road 51, then turn left onto Forest Road 5130 (Eightmile Road) and follow it about 12 miles to the trailhead pullout on the right.
runs: miles to the trailhead pullout on the right

text:
There is more than one gully in the headwall and the choice matters. The northernmost gully is the winter line. In dry conditions take the one trending west toward the upper basin, gained by a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps rather than by a snow chute; in snow conditions the hidden chute goes instead.

From the upper basin, walk south across several gullies before you commit. The correct main couloir is the one that is noticeably narrower than the ones you crossed to get there, and it is the point where crampons go on. A gully you can stroll into without committing is not it — the right one is steep and offers no reprieve from the first steps. Higher, a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave, from where a rightward class 4 traverse on red slabby rock gains the South Ridge of the Main Peak; red rock underfoot on that traverse is the confirmation.
runs: a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave

text: Above the couloir, a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave; an exposed class 4 traverse right on red slabs gains the summit ridge.
runs: a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave

text: Big Four Mountain's first ascent was made July 19, 1931 by Forest Farr and Art Winder via the northwest ridge -- the original route to the summit. As with the mountain's other lines, this route begins from the Big Four viewpoint/ice caves trail approach on the Mountain Loop Highway.
runs: was made july 19 1931 by forest farr and art winder via the northwest ridge

text: First climbed March 2, 1996 by Bart Paull and Doug Littauer in a fast, ultralight, ~9-hour push with no bivy gear. The route starts up an 'ice ribbon' on the initial slabs (thin ice at roughly 65 degrees with a short 85-degree step), continues through the main couloir's three steps of mostly moderate terrain, and hits its crux about three-quarters height: a 100-foot pitch of near-vertical ice leading to steep, often runnelled snow. The upper section mixes rotten ice, shale, and drytooling moves up to roughly 95-degree angles before summit cornices, which may require tunneling through.
runs: a 100 foot pitch of near vertical ice leading to steep

text: The route tops out on the summit ridge well west of the true summit. Descent goes northwest, via rappels and steep downclimbing, to the col between Big Four and Hall Peak; from there, multiple tree-anchored rappels lead back down through the North Face bowl to the base of the face. Careful navigation is essential -- parties have mistakenly descended south instead of northwest in poor visibility.

text: Summit cornices can overhang the face by about six feet. The first ascent cut a tunnel through them with an adze to reach the ridge. The route tops out on the summit ridge well west of the true summit, where a boulder offers a solid cam anchor for bringing up the second.

text: First climbed July 25, 1972 by Ben Guydelkon and Ron Miller as a new line on Big Four's north side. From the end of the ice-caves trail, the party traversed to the northeast side of the first tower to a prominent gully; climbing this gully let them work west onto and up the first tower. They rappelled into a notch, climbed two more towers, then finished with rock scrambling leading to a long, steep, exposed snowfield to the summit.

text: Starting from the Beckey-Tate approach, the route traverses hard right across overlaps to reach a big ledge below an open-book corner. From there it climbs two classic, clean corner pitches — the second through a burly bulge at 5.11c, the route's crux — followed by a wide-crack section, then exits via easier cracks to the top of the wall.
runs: hard right across overlaps to reach a big ledge

text: Located 30 meters right of the Kearney-Thomas start, this variation climbs solid granite splitters and left-facing corners (5.10+) before trending left into a right-facing corner, then joins the Kearney-Thomas line and finishes via a 5.11 finger-crack variation.

text:
Approach exactly as for the East Ridge / Hardscrabble route: walk or bike the gated Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path — half a mile short of the old horse camp, across the road from a large fallen log — and follow the climbers' path east through forest.

The difference is that this route stops at the lower lake rather than continuing to the upper one.

This line sees very few repeat ascents, so beta is thin and any fixed anchors should be treated as unreliable.
runs: across the road from a large fallen log

text: From the gated trailhead, walk or bike the old Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road roughly 7 miles to the unmarked boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes (near the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp). Climb past lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, staying close to the inlet to avoid cliff bands on climber's left. From upper Hardscrabble Lake, climb a gully to a col, drop onto the open granite slab of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit.
runs: onto the open granite slab of the north slope

text: Start at the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate and walk (or mountain-bike) the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about 7 miles to the boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes, which starts roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake, staying near the inlet — straying left leads into cliff bands.
runs: across the road from a large fallen log

text:
Start at the Dingford Creek trailhead gate and walk — or mountain-bike, which is the sensible choice — the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about seven miles.

The boot path for the Hardscrabble Lakes leaves roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers' path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake.

About 20 km and 5,300 ft, and very light foot traffic — do not expect a reliable boot path throughout.
runs: across the road from a large fallen log

text:
The trail departure is marked by a fallen log across the road from it, and it is half a mile short of the Horse Camp. Those two facts together are what make it findable, because the boot path itself is unmarked. If you have reached the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, you have gone about half a mile too far.

The rule that keeps you alive on the way to the lakes: climbing past the lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, stay close to the inlet. Straying left leads into cliff bands, and the east face and buttress above the lower lake drop directly into the water in steep walls. Inlet on your side, cliffs away to the left.

From upper Hardscrabble Lake, the sequence is short and countable: climb a gully to a col, drop onto the open granite slab of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit. Gully, col, granite slab, ridge. If you top the gully and are not looking at an open slab of granite, you are at the wrong col.

What this route is not: the East buttress is a ten-pitch technical line on the same side of the mountain, reached from the lower lake rather than the upper one. If you are roping up, you are on the buttress and not on this route.
runs: onto the open granite slab of the north slope

text: No climbing permit. Camping at Lewis or Wing Lake needs no overnight permit, as both are on national forest land outside the park; a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Rainy Pass.

text: Drive SR-20 to Rainy Pass at about milepost 157.5 and turn into the Rainy Pass Picnic Site on the south side of the highway. The Lake Ann-Maple Pass trailhead (Trail 740) leaves from the paved lot at about 4,855 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park; day passes are sold at the trailhead.

text: Steep start off a left-hand side-pull; plug the #1 Camalot into a pod, clip a bolt, gain a rest ledge, then move left and up through several bolts on a pumpy finish to the anchor.
runs: 1 camalot into a pod clip a bolt

text:
You can see the crag from the car park, and that is the answer in bad weather. The cliff is visible from the west-most parking lots at the Summit West base area. Look at it from the road before you walk in, fix which lump of rock it is, and the walk becomes trivial.

Where it sits relative to the peak: it is an isolated crag, separate from the rest of Guye, low down and near the base of the South Rib. If you are looking at the large west face, this cliff is just around the corner to the right of it and well below. So: west face on your left shoulder, corner, small isolated cliff low on the right.

The move off the ground is the proof, and it is unmistakable. The pitch starts steeply off a left-hand side-pull, and the first piece is a #1 Camalot plugged into a pod, before you clip the first bolt. If there is no pod at head height taking a #1 and no bolt above it, you are at the wrong bit of rock.

And the shape of the whole thing, as a final check: 50 ft, a rest ledge partway up, then a pumpy sequence moving left to a two-bolt chain anchor. It does not top out. Any line here that continues into the mountain above is not this route.

Honest caveat: this is a 2014 line with almost no recorded traffic, so the fixed gear is aging and seldom inspected.
runs: near the base of the south rib if you are looking at the large west face

text: Stay on the ridge following the line of least resistance rather than deviating into adjacent terrain; once you find the ridge crest, navigation is straightforward.
runs: stay on the ridge following the line of least resistance

text: The route has a choose-your-own-adventure feel; multiple lines work; pick the path with the best rock quality and protection opportunities.
runs: the route has a choose your own adventure feel

text:
The first pitch begins at a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and you start just right of it. That patch is the marker the first-ascent party chose to record, and it is the only thing at the base of this wall that is a shape rather than a description. Walk the talus until you find it.

The positive test is a colour change, and it is excellent in bad light: pitch one is a 220 ft scramble at about 5.4 up white slabs to a stance below a large, steeper band of darker rock. White below, dark above, easy climbing. If your first pitch is hard, or if the rock is uniform, you are somewhere else.

The second confirmation is above the first: from that stance you are aiming for an obvious, large open book, which takes the second pitch at 5.8. A big open corner directly above easy white slabs is the pair of features that identifies this route. One without the other is not enough.

Left to right across this wall, facing it from the west: Oregonian, Soviet, Cascadian. This is the right-hand one — looker's right of both older routes, which are on the north-west buttress and are out of view at the far left margin of the wall from here. If you can see two other lines to your left and none to your right, you are in the correct place.

The negative marker is the strongest on this page, and it is about what lies further right: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the long snowfield, is unclimbed, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious. This route begins just right of a tiny snowpatch, not above a long one. If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.

Where it eases: difficulties relent only on reaching the ridge just south of the true summit, sixteen pitches up. There is no midway escape.
runs: you are aiming for an obvious large open book
reaching the ridge just south of the true summit

text: Bonanza Peak (9,516') is the highest non-volcanic summit in Washington and the highpoint of Chelan County. The Mary Green Glacier route — first climbed in 1937 by Curtis Ijames, Barrie James, and Joe Leuthold (Mazamas) — is the peak's classic standard line, ascending its eastern side. Reached only via the Lady of the Lake ferry up Lake Chelan and the remote trail-and-boat village of Holden, the climb combines glacier travel and a moat crossing with a short, exposed Class 3-4 rock finish to a summit deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. From the Holden Campground trailhead it's roughly 14 miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of elevation gain to the summit, on top of the multi-day boat-and-trail approach just to reach that trailhead.
runs: is the highest non volcanic summit in washington and

text: First ascended by Seth Keena and Erik Bonnett in early September 2013 (ascent dated 9/4/2013). Rated V, 5.9+, 2,200 ft total: 1,600 ft of new terrain (mostly sustained 5.6-5.8 with moves to 5.9+, via ramp/ledge systems) then 600 ft shared with the Soviet Route to the summit. It begins a few hundred yards left of the Soviet Route, making the Soviet and Oregonian the two established lines on this northwest wall. The first-ascent team's approach that year was an unusually long ~32-mile one-way trip (including ~10 miles of biking) due to ferry/road closures in effect at the time - this is not the standard approach.

text: From a camp near the head of Park Creek, climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, then go left up the glacier to an icefall and traverse right through and under it (reported as a genuinely exposed, 'frightening' crossing) to reach the main rock wall. Follow a prominent central rib essentially straight up the face on generally sound Cascade granodiorite/orthogneiss, through a crumbly red rock stratum that crosses the whole face at roughly mid-height, to a 100-foot notch near the summit, then on to the top. The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 feet high.

text:
A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend left up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse right through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.
runs: small glacier at the base of the face

text: Climb the first three pitches of the Southwest Rib, then go left at a ledge. A short, loose 5.2 pitch leads to a belay below the roofs; the money pitch pulls under and over double roofs at 5.10b with good gear, followed by an easy chimney into 5.9 thin hands to a ledge with great position, joining the upper Southwest Rib/South Arete descent.

text:
This route has no ground start, and that is the most important fact about finding it. You reach it by climbing the first three pitches of the southwest rib, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and then going left at a ledge where the two roofs come into view.

So the base of the day is the base of the southwest rib, and that has a landmark you can stand under: the Y-shaped larch tree at the base of the southwest rib, left of the southwest couloir. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

The in-route test is visual and binary: go left at the ledge where the two roofs come into view. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A hazard right at the start of the pitch, recorded because it is exactly where a party is committing: there is a loose block right at the start of the roof pitch.

What nobody does here, which answers the obvious question: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the rabbit ears then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted stations climber's right of the gully, which land at the foot of the South Arete rather than back at the larch.
runs: the first three pitches of the southwest rib
